Infant Head Tilt and Flat Head: Which Way Does the Ear Point?

The tilt names the tight muscle; the ear names the flat head

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line
  • Head tilts toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass that appears at 1 to 4 weeks and does not transilluminate, chin turned away: congenital muscular torticollis; the muscle bends the head toward itself and turns the chin away. Clinical diagnosis; stretching, repositioning, tummy time and physical therapy. Late treatment leaves permanent craniofacial asymmetry.
  • Flat occiput, ear on that side forward (parallelogram): positional plagiocephaly, from supine sleep, a neck that turns one way or prematurity. Reposition; no imaging.
  • Flat occiput, ear pushed back with a ridge (trapezoid): lambdoid craniosynostosis. Head CT (computed tomography) and craniofacial referral.

Breech, oligohydramnios or twins (intrauterine crowding): examine the hips and feet; hip dysplasia, metatarsus adductus and clubfoot travel with torticollis.

A new tilt in an older child with any neurologic sign is a posterior fossa tumor until MRI (magnetic resonance imaging).

Diagnosis
Flat back of the head: look down from above and find the ear on the flat side
DiagnosisEar on the flat sideHead seen from above, and the clue
Positional plagiocephalyPushed forwardParallelogram: the flat back and the same-side forehead both shift forward; no ridge
Lambdoid craniosynostosisPulled backTrapezoid: no forehead shift; a hard ridge over the fused suture
Torticollis with positional flatteningPushed forwardParallelogram, flat on the side the chin turns to (opposite the tight muscle); head tilts toward a firm neck-muscle mass
Neck-mass mimics Cystic hygroma – lymphatic malformation, linked to aneuploidy; soft, fluctuant, posterior triangle, transilluminates · Cervical lymphadenitis – tender, warm node outside the muscle, often with fever · Clavicle fracture – after shoulder dystocia; crepitus and an arm not moving, not a tilt
Management and treatment
Management ladder: torticollis and flat head
TrackInterventionEscalate when
Flat headRepositioning and tummy timeNot better in 4 to 8 weeks: image the sutures; if open, a helmet for severe flattening
Tight muscleStretching and physical therapyNo improvement by 6 months of age: pediatric orthopedics; release, usually after 12 months, in the 5 to 10% that fail
Practice
  1. 2-month-old girl, born breech, with a flat right occiput neck mass first felt at 3 weeks; right ear forward head tilts left; chin turns right Firm, painless left sternocleidomastoid mass; does not transilluminate T 37.0 °C · hips stable → Congenital muscular torticollis → tilt toward a firm sternocleidomastoid mass with the chin turned away is congenital muscular torticollis; the flat head with the ear forward is positional, from lying one way; stretching, repositioning, tummy time
  2. 3-month-old girl with a flat right occiput right ear and forehead sit forward sleeps on her back; full neck rotation No neck mass or ridge T 36.9 °C · head circumference 50th percentile → Positional plagiocephaly → a flat occiput with the ear and forehead forward (a parallelogram) is positional plagiocephaly: repositioning and tummy time, no imaging
  3. 4-month-old boy with a flat right occiput right ear sits behind the left palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture No neck mass; full neck rotation T 37.0 °C · head circumference 40th percentile → Craniosynostosis → a flat occiput with the ear pushed back and a ridge (a trapezoid) is lambdoid craniosynostosis: head CT and craniofacial referral
  4. Newborn girl with a neck mass noted at birth soft, fluctuant, in the posterior triangle the mass transilluminates Head held midline; no tilt T 36.8 °C · feeding and breathing normally → Cystic hygroma → a soft posterior-triangle mass that transilluminates is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation), linked to aneuploidy; the torticollis mass is firm and does not transilluminate
  5. 8-year-old boy with 3 weeks of a new head tilt morning headaches; vomits on waking papilledema on fundoscopy Left sixth nerve palsy: cannot abduct the left eye T 37.0 °C · no neck mass or fever → Posterior fossa tumor → an acquired head tilt with any neurologic sign in an older child is a posterior fossa tumor until imaged: MRI of the brain
  6. 2-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis today born breech at term head tilts right; chin turns left; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass Feet look normal T 37.0 °C · hip exam equivocal → Hip ultrasound → torticollis and breech both come from intrauterine crowding, which also causes hip dysplasia: screen the hips with ultrasound (a Melbourne children's hospital guideline recommends it for torticollis; breech alone also qualifies)
  7. 2-month-old girl with a head tilt to the right since birth born breech; firm right sternocleidomastoid mass left hip clunks on Barlow, reduces on Ortolani Left thigh folds asymmetric T 37.0 °C · no hip swelling or warmth → Developmental dysplasia of the hip → a dislocatable hip that reduces in an infant is developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), part of the crowding picture: Pavlik harness; the tilt and mass are the torticollis
  8. 6-month-old girl was diagnosed with congenital muscular torticollis at 2 months 3 months of daily stretching and physical therapy tilt and limited rotation unchanged Sternocleidomastoid still tight T 37.0 °C · no neurologic signs → Refer to pediatric orthopedics → most torticollis resolves with stretching; no significant improvement by 6 months of age goes to pediatric orthopedics for evaluation, rather than 6 more months of the same; release, usually after 12 months, is for the 5 to 10% that fail
Pairs with Brachial Plexus Injury at Birth: the newborn who will not move an arm. Posterior Fossa Localization: the acquired tilt with cranial nerve signs. Posterior Urethral Valves and Potter Sequence: the same constraint physiology.
Transferable rule

The underlying cause explains every finding: crowding gives the tilt and the hip, and the tilt gives the flat head; reject a diagnosis that leaves one out.
